ECE 6390 / Digital signals

Pulse width and spectrum

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how making a pulse shorter in time expands its spectrum.

A transmitter needs a pulse that fits its channel bandwidth. For a rectangular pulse with amplitude A and duration T, the Fourier transform is X(f) = AT sinc(fT). Here f is in cycles per second and sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx).

The first zeros occur at f = ±1/T. Abrupt time edges create sidelobes extending indefinitely in frequency, so an ideal rectangular pulse has no finite strict bandwidth. Practical filters smooth the edges and reshape the pulse, which can make adjacent pulses overlap.

The displayed spectrum retains its sign. Negative spectral amplitude represents a π phase reversal; spectral power is proportional to |X(f)|². Pulse energy also depends on amplitude and load, so V²·time should be converted through a specified resistance before calling it joules.

Example

A 1 ms pulse has its first spectral zeros at ±1 kHz. Reducing duration to 0.5 ms moves the first zeros to ±2 kHz. At fixed amplitude the pulse contains less energy and has a smaller DC Fourier amplitude AT.

    Practice

    1. Halve pulse duration while keeping amplitude fixed. What happens to the first zero and to the pulse voltage-squared integral?

    The zero scales as 1/T; the integral is A²T.

    The first-zero frequency doubles. The voltage-squared integral halves.

    2. Does the first spectral zero mean that no spectral energy exists beyond that frequency?

    Look at the sidelobes after the first zero.

    No. The sinc spectrum has further lobes. The first-zero bandwidth is a useful measure of the main lobe, not a strict spectral support boundary.
